GegenNet: Spectral Convolutional Neural Networks for Link Sign Prediction in Signed Bipartite Graphs

Conference: Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management; November 10–14, 2025; Seoul, Republic of KoreaProceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’25), November 10–14, 2025, Seoul, Republic of KoreaDOI: 10.1145/3746252.3761129ISBN: 979-8-4007-2040-6/2025/11CCS: Computing methodologies Supervised learning by classificationCCS: Computing methodologies Neural networksCCS: Mathematics of computing Graph theory
Hewen Wang Note: Both authors contributed equally to the paper. Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore email: wanghewen@u.nus.edu , Renchi Yang Affiliation: Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong SAR, China email: renchi@hkbu.edu.hk and Xiaokui Xiao Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore email: xkxiao@nus.edu.sg

Abstract.

Given a signed bipartite graph (SBG) 𝒢\mathcal{G} with two disjoint node sets 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the goal of link sign prediction is to predict the signs of potential links connecting 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} based on known positive and negative edges in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The majority of existing solutions towards link sign prediction mainly focus on unipartite signed graphs, which are sub-optimal due to the neglect of node heterogeneity and unique bipartite characteristics of SBGs. To this end, recent studies adapt graph neural networks to SBGs by introducing message-passing schemes for both inter-partition (𝒰×𝒱\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{V}) and intra-partition (𝒰×𝒰\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{U} or 𝒱×𝒱\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}) node pairs. However, the fundamental spectral convolutional operators were originally designed for positive links in unsigned graphs, and thus, are not optimal for inferring missing positive or negative links from known ones in SBGs.

Motivated by this, this paper proposes GegenNet, a novel and effective spectral convolutional neural network model for link sign prediction in SBGs. In particular, GegenNet achieves enhanced model capacity and high predictive accuracy through three main technical contributions: (i) fast and theoretically grounded spectral decomposition techniques for node feature initialization; (ii) a new spectral graph filter based on the Gegenbauer polynomial basis; and (iii) multi-layer sign-aware spectral convolutional networks alternating Gegenbauer polynomial filters with positive and negative edges. Our extensive empirical studies reveal that GegenNet can achieve significantly superior performance (up to a gain of 4.28%4.28\% in AUC and 11.69%11.69\% in F1) in link sign prediction compared to 11 strong competitors over 6 benchmark SBG datasets.

Keywords: 
link sign prediction, spectral graph filter, bipartite graphs

1. Introduction

Signed bipartite graphs (SBGs) are an expressive data structure for modeling positive and negative interactions between two heterogeneous sets of real-world entities. Such graph data is prevalent in practical domains such as recommendation systems, sentiment analysis, and opinion mining, where users may express positive or negative sentiments toward items or other entities. On top of that, SBGs enable the modeling of complex social and economic interactions, such as trust/distrust relationships in e-commerce platforms or like/dislike actions in social networks. A fundamental task in SBGs is to predict the signs of potential links, i.e., link sign prediction, which finds numerous applications in online social media (Leskovec et al., 2010), recommender systems (Massa and Avesani, 2007), and so on. Distinct from traditional link prediction in general graphs, link sign prediction in SBGs additionally poses challenges in coping with node heterogeneity, lopsided structure, and the presence of positive and negative links.

In the literature (Zhang et al., 2024), the majority of existing works (Rizi and Granitzer, 2020; Islam et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2018; Javari et al., 2020; Cucuringu et al., 2020; Rizi and Granitzer, 2020; Derr et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020a; Huang et al., 2019a; Huang et al., 2021b; He et al., 2022b) towards link sign prediction primarily focus on unipartite signed graphs and resort to learning node representations using approaches based on Skip-gram models (Mikolov et al., 2013) (e.g., DeepWalk, node2vec) or graph neural networks (GNNs) (Kipf and Welling, 2017). As reviewed in Section 2.2, most recent advances (Zhang et al., 2024) are GNN-based, all of which strongly rely on the message-passing paradigm (Huang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021) or attention mechanisms that are originally dedicated for unsigned unipartite networks that solely consist of positive edges. Moreover, the design of most of them follows principles including balance theory (Cartwright and Harary, 1956) and status theory (Leskovec et al., 2010), where the former postulates that “the friend of my friend is my friend” and “the enemy of my enemy is my friend”, while the latter explains social hierarchies and authority relationships. However, the direct adoption of these techniques for SBGs is inappropriate since an SBG consists of two heterogeneous sets of nodes and positive/negative links connecting them, which render traditional principles insufficient to capture the complex relations and interplay among the nodes.

Recently, a few attempts have been made to address the unique challenges of link sign prediction in SBGs. More precisely, Huang et al. (2021a) extend the balance theory to SBGs through the inter- and intra-partition perspectives and re-design the message functions to aggregate information from different sets (i.e., inter- and intra-partition) of neighborhoods. To deal with noisy interactions present in real SBGs, Zhang et al. (2023) introduce the contrastive learning mechanism to learn robust node representations, in which a multi-perspective contrastive loss is optimized over augmented graphs created from the inter- and intra-partition perspectives. By modeling explicit and implicit relations between the inter- and intra-partition nodes, these two approaches are enabled to capture node heterogeneity and bipartite structure in SBGs, and hence, achieve encouraging performance in predicting link signs. However, akin to their unipartite counterparts, these models are sub-optimal as the adopted spectral convolutional (message-passing) operations are catered for positive edges and depend on the monomial bases. There is still a lack of discussion on the design choices of such foundational operators for both positive and negative links in SBGs.

In response, in this paper, we present GegenNet, an effective spectral convolutional neural network specifically designed for link sign prediction in SBGs. To deepen the understanding of the relations between positive and negative links in SBGs, we recast the link sign prediction task into four curving fitting problems with known and missing links based on our theoretical transformations. Our empirical observations on real SBGs manifest that existing graph filters based on monomial bases often struggle with capturing both low- and high-frequency spectral signals in SBGs, which motivates the design of our novel spectral graph filter built on the Gegenbauer polynomial basis. Based thereon, GegenNet stacks multiple layers of sign-aware spectral convolutional operators with positive and negative links severally using various Gegenbauer polynomial bases, leading to a sophisticated combination that greatly enhances model capacity as pinpointed by our theoretical analysis. Further, instead of randomly initializing node features as in prior works, which engenders suboptimal feature representations and hinders the effective utilization of graph structure, GegenNet includes efficacious spectral decomposition techniques that allow us to efficiently construct high-quality initial node embeddings encoding inter- and intra-partition relations between nodes. In summary, our major contributions of this paper are:

  • •

    Spectral Feature Initialization for SBGs: We develop an effective feature initialization method that can accurately encode structural semantics in SBGs into node embeddings through fast and theoretically grounded spectral decompositions.

  • •

    New Spectral Graph Filter for SBGs: We design a new spectral graph filter based on the Gegenbauer polynomial basis, which overcomes the limitations of previous graph filters.

  • •

    Sign-aware Spectral Convolutional Layers for SBGs: We propose GegenNet that comprises multiple layers of spectral convolutional neural networks using Gegenbauer polynomial filters over positive and negative links in a separate, alternate, and unified manner for stronger model capacity.

  • •

    Comprehensive Evaluation: Extensive experiments comparing GegenNet against 11 baselines are conducted on 6 real SBG datasets, exhibiting the remarkable superiority of GegenNet over the state of the art in link sign prediction.

2. Related Work

2.1. Bipartite Graph Representation Learning

Existing works for bipartite graph representation learning can be categorized into proximity-preserving and message-passing approaches, where the former seeks to capture both local and global proximity among nodes (Yang and Shi, 2024), while the latter applies the message-passing paradigm in GNNs to bipartite networks.

More specifically, BiNE (Gao et al., 2018) extends random walk-based Skip-gram models (Mikolov et al., 2013) to non-attributed bipartite graphs. BiANE (Huang et al., 2020) leverages autoencoders to integrate structural and attribute information by considering intra- and inter-domain proximities severally. FOBE and HOBE (Sybrandt and Safro, 2020) preserve type-specific semantic information in bipartite graphs by sampling nodes using different proximities. GEBE (Yang et al., 2022) decomposes proximity matrices capturing multi-hop connectivity among homogeneous and heterogeneous nodes. EAGLE (Wang et al., 2024) leverages the factorized feature propagation (FFP) scheme to incorporate long-range dependencies of edges/features.

Amid message-passing-based methods, Cascade-BGNN (He et al., 2020) combines a self-supervised framework with inter- and intra-domain aggregation mechanisms. BiGI (Cao et al., 2021) applies a subgraph-level attention mechanism to maximize the mutual information between local and global node embeddings. DualHGCN (Xue et al., 2021) transforms multiplex bipartite networks into homogeneous hypergraphs and utilizes spectral convolutional operators to capture within- and cross-domain information. Lastly, AnchorGNN (Wu et al., 2023) proposes a global-local learning framework with an anchor-based message-passing schema (Zhou et al., 2023).

2.2. Signed Graph Representation Learning

Unlike traditional graph representation learning methods for unsigned graphs, signed graph representation learning (SGRL) encodes nodes and edges into low-dimensional representations in the presence of the co-existence of positive ties (e.g., trust and friendship) and negative ties (e.g., distrust and enmity). Existing works towards SGRL can be mainly categorized into two classes: random walk-based and GNN-based methods.

In particular, random walk-based approaches generate node sequences by traversing the graph and input such sequences into Skip-Gram models (Mikolov et al., 2013) for representation learning. These methods incorporate the signs of edges to capture both positive and negative relationships. Representative methods include SNE (Rizi and Granitzer, 2020), SIGNet (Islam et al., 2018), and SIDE (Kim et al., 2018). Signed GNNs extend classic GNN architectures to handle signed graphs by incorporating balance and status theories into the message-passing process. SGCN (Derr et al., 2018) utilizes dual representations to handle balanced and unbalanced relationships. SNEA (Li et al., 2020a) applies attention mechanisms for weighted aggregation of neighborhood information, while SiGAT (Huang et al., 2019a) incorporates motif-based attention to capture structural properties of signed networks. More models can be found in a recent review (Zhang et al., 2024).

Recently, several GNN models (Huang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2023) specially designed for SBGs have been proposed. More concretely, SBGNN (Huang et al., 2021a) incorporates the balance theory and bipartite nature into the message-passing scheme. SBGCL (Zhang et al., 2023) resorts to contrastive learning over perturbed graphs constructed from the SBGs from the perspectives of inter- and intra-partition.

3. Preliminaries

Problem Statement. Given an SBG 𝒢=(𝒰,𝒱,ℰ(+),ℰ(−))\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}^{(+)},\mathcal{E}^{(-)}), link sign prediction problem aims at predicting if a pair of nodes (ui,vj)∈𝒰×𝒱(u_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{V} will be disconnected or connected by a positive or negative link. Mathematically, for any possible link (ui,vj)(u_{i},v_{j}), its goal is to find a mapping function F⁡(ui,vj)→{1,−1}F(u_{i},v_{j})\rightarrow\{1,-1\}.

3.2. Link Prediction Heuristics

A common way for link predictions is to calculate the proximity p⁡(vi,vj)p(v_{i},v_{j}) for any node pair (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}) over the input graph (Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, 2003). Canonical proximity measures in general (unsigned) graphs can be classified into two major categories: local and global heuristics (Lü and Zhou, 2011), where the former primarily rely on common direct neighbors for measuring node proximity, while the latter exploit the high-order topological connectivity between nodes. The representative of local heuristics is the number of common neighbors:

p⁡(vi,vj)=|𝒩⁡(vi)∩𝒩⁡(vj)|=𝐀i,j2,p(v_{i},v_{j})=|\mathcal{N}(v_{i})\cap\mathcal{N}(v_{j})|=\mathbf{A}^{2}_{i,j},

where 𝒩⁡(vi)\mathcal{N}(v_{i}) denotes the number of neighbors of viv_{i} and 𝐀\mathbf{A} is the symmetric adjacency matrix of the graph. Classic global heuristics include the kk-hop random walks (kk-hop RW)  (Lovász, 1993), personalized PageRank (PPR) (Jeh and Widom, 2003), and heat kernel PageRank (HKPR) (Chung, 2007), etc., whose matrix forms are displayed in Table 1, where 𝐀^\hat{\mathbf{A}} represents the normalized adjacency matrix of the graph11 1 In standard PPR and HKPR, 𝐀^\hat{\mathbf{A}} is usually the transition matrix of the graph. and 𝐀^i,j\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{i,j} signifies the probability of a random walk from viv_{i} visits vjv_{j} at kk-th step.

4. Methodology

This section presents our GegenNet model for link sign prediction in SBGs. More concretely, GegenNet includes KK layers of sign-aware spectral convolutional operations that are built on our Gegenbauer polynomial-based spectral graph filters (Sections 4.1 and 4.2), our spectral decomposition approaches for initializing node features by extracting inter- and intra-partition patterns from SBGs (Section 4.3), as well as the model training objective in Section 4.4.

4.1. Design of Spectral Graph Filters

Instead of employing classic spectral graph filters that are merely designed for positive links, this section investigates the design of the filter g𝜽​(𝚲)g_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) for SBGs on the basis of theoretical analyses and empirical observations pertaining to the relations between observed and future positive/negative edges, respectively.

4.1.1. Spectral Transformation of Link Sign Prediction

The link sign prediction task can be framed as looking for functions that map known links to the missing links with minimal error. Since there are positive and negative links in both training sets 𝐀^+\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+}, 𝐀^−\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-} and test sets 𝐘+\mathbf{Y}^{+}, 𝐘−\mathbf{Y}^{-}, there are four possible functions, i.e., f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot), f(−−)(⋅)f^{(--)}(\cdot), f(−+)(⋅)f^{(-+)}(\cdot), and f(+−)(⋅)f^{(+-)}(\cdot). minf(−+)∈ℱ∥f(−+)(𝐀^−)−𝐘+∥F⇔∑i=1|𝒰|+|𝒱|(f(−+)(𝚲i,i−)−𝐔⋅,i−⊤𝐘+𝐔⋅,i−)2,\displaystyle\min_{f^{(-+)}\in\mathcal{F}}{\|f^{(-+)}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})-\mathbf{Y}^{+}\|_{F}}\Leftrightarrow{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|}{(f^{(-+)}({\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i,i}}^{-})-{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{+}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-})^{2}}},
minf(−−)∈ℱ∥f(−−)(𝐀^−)−𝐘−∥F⇔∑i=1|𝒰|+|𝒱|(f(−−)(𝚲i,i−)−𝐔⋅,i−⊤𝐘−𝐔⋅,i−)2,\displaystyle\min_{f^{(--)}\in\mathcal{F}}{\|f^{(--)}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})-\mathbf{Y}^{-}\|_{F}}\Leftrightarrow{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|}{(f^{(--)}({\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i,i}}^{-})-{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{-}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-})^{2}}},
minf(+−)∈ℱ∥f(+−)(𝐀^+)−𝐘−∥F⇔∑i=1|𝒰|+|𝒱|(f(+−)(𝚲i,i+)−𝐔⋅,i+⊤𝐘−𝐔⋅,i+)2.\displaystyle\min_{f^{(+-)}\in\mathcal{F}}{\|f^{(+-)}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})-\mathbf{Y}^{-}\|_{F}}\Leftrightarrow{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|}{(f^{(+-)}({\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i,i}}^{+})-{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{-}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+})^{2}}}.

4.1.2. Curve Fitting with Spectral Filtering Functions

Based on the above spectral transformations, the choice of transformation functions f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot), f(−−)(⋅)f^{(--)}(\cdot), f(−+)(⋅)f^{(-+)}(\cdot), and f(+−)(⋅)f^{(+-)}(\cdot) for link sign prediction can be reduced to a least-squares curve fitting problem. Take f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot) as an example. Intuitively, when we let eigenvalues 𝚲i,i+{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i,i}}^{+} (1≤i≤|𝒰|+|𝒱|1\leq i\leq|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|) be the xx-axis, the curve of an ideal f(++)(𝚲i,i+)f^{(++)}({\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i,i}}^{+}) should fit the curve of 𝐔⋅,i+⊤​𝐘+​𝐔⋅,i+{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{+}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+}. Doing so facilitates us to find spectral filters that are best suited to the link sign prediction by empirical observations on real SBGs.

Inspired by this, on the MLM and House1to10 datasets (Table 3), we empirically study the choices of f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot), f(−−)(⋅)f^{(--)}(\cdot), f(−+)(⋅)f^{(-+)}(\cdot), and f(+−)(⋅)f^{(+-)}(\cdot) using the five spectral filtering functions g𝜽​(⋅)g_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot) adopted in GCN/SGC, APPNP, GDC, GNN-LF, and GNN-HF with hyperparameters suggested in their respective papers (see Table 2), respectively. In particular, we refer to the regions where eigenvalues with small (near −1.0-1.0), middle (roughly within the interval [−0.2,0.2][-0.2,0.2]), and large values (near 1.01.0), as high-, mid-, and low-frequency areas, respectively, and their corresponding ideal values as high-, mid-, and low-frequency signals, respectively (Shuman et al., 2013). According to Fig. 1, we can make the following observations.

  • •

    𝐔⋅,i+⊤​𝐘+​𝐔⋅,i+{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{+}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+} and 𝐔⋅,i−⊤​𝐘−​𝐔⋅,i−{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{-}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-} are negatively correlated to the eigenvalues in 𝚲+{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{+} and 𝚲−{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-}, respectively, when they are in the mid-frequency area, but are positively correlated to the eigenvalues in the high- and low-frequency areas.

  • •

    In comparison, 𝐔⋅,i+⊤​𝐘−​𝐔⋅,i+{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{-}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{+} (resp. 𝐔⋅,i−⊤​𝐘+​𝐔⋅,i−{{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-}}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}^{+}{\mathbf{U}}_{\cdot,i}^{-}) exhibits completely opposite behaviors to the eigenvalues in 𝚲+{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{+} (resp. 𝚲−{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-}).

  • •

    The curves by the spectral filtering functions closely approximate the ideal curves in the mid-frequency area, but deviate significantly from them with opposite trends outside this region.

The above phenomenon indicates that existing spectral filters g𝜽​(⋅)g_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot) are incompetent for capturing low- and high-frequency signals in both positive and negative links. Their limited expressive power can be ascribed to the fact that they are composed of a series of monomial bases that are not orthogonal to each other w.r.t. weight functions (Wang and Zhang, 2022).

4.1.3. Gegenbauer Polynomial Filters

In response, we propose to employ the complex and orthogonal polynomial, i.e., the Gegenbauer polynomial function, as the transformation functions f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot), f(−−)(⋅)f^{(--)}(\cdot), f(−+)(⋅)f^{(-+)}(\cdot), and f(+−)(⋅)f^{(+-)}(\cdot). Specifically, given a diagonal matrix 𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda} containing eigenvalues, its Gegenbauer polynomial bases are defined in a recursive form:

(6) Jα0(𝚲)=𝐈,Jα1(𝚲)=(α+12)⋅𝚲,k≥2,Jkα​(𝚲)=ωk​𝚲⋅Jk−1α​(𝚲)−ωk′⋅Jk−2α​(𝚲),\begin{gathered}J^{\alpha}_{0}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=\mathbf{I},\ J^{\alpha}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=\left(\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{\Lambda},\\ \text{$k\geq 2$},\ J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=\omega_{k}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-1}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})-\omega_{k}^{\prime}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-2}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}),\end{gathered}

where the coefficient α≥−12\alpha\geq-\frac{1}{2} and weights satisfy

ωk=(2​k+2​α−1)​(k+α−1)k⁡(k+2​α−1)​and​ωk′=(k+α−12)​(k+α−32)k⁡(k+2​α−1).\begin{gathered}\omega_{k}=\frac{(2k+2\alpha-1)(k+\alpha-1)}{k(k+2\alpha-1)}\ \text{and}\ \omega_{k}^{\prime}=\frac{(k+\alpha-\frac{1}{2})(k+\alpha-\frac{3}{2})}{k(k+2\alpha-1)}.\end{gathered}
Theorem 4.2.

For K≥ℕ0K\geq\mathbb{N}_{0} and α,a≥−12\alpha,a\geq-\frac{1}{2}, the Gegenbauer polynomial basis JKα​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) is a KK-order Gegenbauer polynomial, i.e., JKα​(𝚲)=∑k=0KckK⋅Jka​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=\sum_{k=0}^{K}{c_{k}^{K}\cdot J^{a}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})}, where ckKc_{k}^{K} is the polynomial coefficient.

Theorem 4.2 indicates that the kk-th Gegenbauer polynomial basis Jkα​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) is equivalent to a kk-order Gegenbauer polynomial, which implies that we can directly adopt Jkα​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) as the spectral filtering function, and hence, the transformation functions f(++)(⋅)f^{(++)}(\cdot), f(−−)(⋅)f^{(--)}(\cdot), f(−+)(⋅)f^{(-+)}(\cdot), and f(+−)(⋅)f^{(+-)}(\cdot). Accordingly, the corresponding spectral graph filters g𝜽​(⋅)g_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot) for positive and negative links are defined as in the following recursive form33 3 The closed-form expression can be found in Appendix B.

(7) Jα0(𝐀^+)=𝐈,Jα1(𝐀^+)=(α+1)⋅𝐀^+,Jαk(𝐀^+)=ωk𝐀^+⋅Jαk−1(𝐀^+)−ωk′⋅Jαk−2(𝐀^+)∀k≥2,and\begin{gathered}J^{\alpha}_{0}({\hat{\mathbf{A}}}^{+})=\mathbf{I},\ J^{\alpha}_{1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})=({\alpha+1})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+},\\ J^{\alpha}_{k}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})=\omega_{k}\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})-\omega_{k}^{\prime}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-2}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})\ \forall{k\geq 2},\ \text{and}\end{gathered}
(8) Jα0(𝐀^−)=𝐈,Jα1(𝐀^−)=(α+1)⋅𝐀^−,Jαk(𝐀^−)=ωk𝐀^−⋅Jαk−1(𝐀^−)−ωk′⋅Jαk−2(𝐀^−)∀k≥2.\begin{gathered}J^{\alpha}_{0}({\hat{\mathbf{A}}}^{-})=\mathbf{I},\ J^{\alpha}_{1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})=({\alpha+1})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-},\\ J^{\alpha}_{k}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})=\omega_{k}\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})-\omega_{k}^{\prime}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k-2}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})\ \forall{k\geq 2}.\end{gathered}

As plotted in Fig. 1, we can observe that the Gegenbauer polynomial basis Jkα​(⋅)J^{\alpha}_{k}(\cdot) well fits the target curves in the four cases when α=1.0\alpha=1.0 and k=3k=3, especially in the low- and high-frequency areas, demonstrating its high efficacy in link sign prediction on SBGs.

Remark. Gegenbauer polynomials generalize other well-known polynomials, i.e.,

  • •

    When α=0\alpha=0 or 1.01.0, Jkα​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) is Chebyshev polynomials;

  • •

    When α=0.5\alpha=0.5, Jkα​(𝚲)J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) is Legendre polynomials.

4.2. Sign-aware Spectral Convolutional Layers

We denote by 𝐇(ℓ)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} (0≤ℓ≤L−10\leq\ell\leq L-1) the output node embeddings at the ℓ\ell-th layer of the GegenNet model. Initially,

𝐇(0)=𝐗𝐖(0),\mathbf{H}^{(0)}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{(0)},

where 𝐖(0)\mathbf{W}^{(0)} is learnable parameters and 𝐗\mathbf{X} denotes the spectral node features extracted from the input graph topology 𝐀(+)\mathbf{A}^{(+)} and 𝐀(−)\mathbf{A}^{(-)}. The construction of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is deferred to the succeeding section. As pinpointed in the preceding section, both the positive and negative links in 𝒢\mathcal{G} are conducive to the prediction of unknown links in 𝐘+\mathbf{Y}^{+} and 𝐘−\mathbf{Y}^{-}, respectively. As such, at the (ℓ+1)(\ell+1)-th layer, GegenNet creates 𝐇pos(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}} and 𝐇neg(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}} by applying our Gegenbauer polynomial filter Jℓ+1αJ^{\alpha}_{\ell+1} on 𝐇(ℓ)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} with 𝐀^+\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+} and 𝐀^−\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-}, respectively, as follows:

(9) 𝐇pos(ℓ+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}} =PReLU​(δ⋅Jℓ+1α​(𝐀^+)​𝐇(ℓ)​𝐖pos(ℓ+1))\displaystyle=\textsf{PReLU}(\delta\cdot J^{\alpha}_{\ell+1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}})
𝐇neg(ℓ+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}} =PReLU​(δ⋅Jℓ+1α​(𝐀^−)​𝐇(ℓ)​𝐖neg(ℓ+1)),\displaystyle=\textsf{PReLU}(\delta\cdot J^{\alpha}_{\ell+1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}}),

where 𝐖pos(ℓ+1)\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}} and 𝐖neg(ℓ+1)\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}} are layer-specific learnable weights, δ\delta is a weight hyperparameter, and PReLU​(⋅)\textsf{PReLU}(\cdot) stands for the parametric ReLU, i.e., the non-linear activation function. Intuitively, 𝐇pos(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}} (resp. 𝐇neg(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}}) encodes both structural connectivity and positive (resp. negative) relationships from 𝐀^+\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+} (resp. 𝐀^−\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-}). Apart from them, we further apply a non-linear transformation on 𝐇(ℓ)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} to get

(10) 𝐇org(ℓ+1)=PReLU​(𝐇(ℓ)​𝐖org(ℓ+1)),\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{org}}=\textsf{PReLU}(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{org}}),

which carries the accumulated information in the past.

In turn, as in Eq. (11), the node embeddings 𝐇(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)} output at the (ℓ+1)(\ell+1)-th model layer is obtained by fusing 𝐇org(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{org}}, 𝐇pos(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}} and 𝐇neg(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}} via a concatenation, followed by a linear transformation with learnable weights 𝐖cat(ℓ+1)\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{cat}}.

(11) 𝐇(ℓ+1)=(𝐇org(ℓ+1)∥𝐇pos(ℓ+1)∥𝐇neg(ℓ+1))⋅𝐖cat(ℓ+1)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}=\left(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{org}}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}}\right)\cdot\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{cat}}

In doing so, GegenNet is able to inject sign-aware structural information and their sophisticated fusion and interactions into the node embeddings. The output 𝐇(ℓ)\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} at the LL-th layer is used as the final node representations 𝐙\mathbf{Z} for nodes in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

𝐇(ℓ+1)=\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)}= Jℓ+1α​(𝐀^+)​𝐇(ℓ)​𝐖pos(ℓ+1)​𝐖cat,pos(ℓ+1)+Jℓ+1α​(𝐀^−)​𝐇(ℓ)​𝐖neg(ℓ+1)​𝐖cat,neg(ℓ+1)\displaystyle J^{\alpha}_{\ell+1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+})\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{pos}}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{cat},\text{pos}}+J^{\alpha}_{\ell+1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{neg}}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)}_{\text{cat},\text{neg}}

+𝐗𝐖(0)​𝐖org(1)​𝐖cat,org(1)\displaystyle+\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{(0)}\mathbf{W}^{(1)}_{\text{org}}\mathbf{W}^{(1)}_{\text{cat},\text{org}}

and 𝒫(ℓ)={Jℓα​(𝐀+^),Jℓα​(𝐀−^),𝐈}, 1≤ℓ≤L\mathcal{P}^{(\ell)}=\{J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}^{+}}),J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}^{-}}),\mathbf{I}\},\ 1\leq\ell\leq L, we can derive that

𝐙=𝐇(L)=∑𝐏(1)∈𝒫(1)⋯∑𝐏(L)∈𝒫(L)(∏ℓ=1L𝐏(ℓ))𝐗⋅W(𝐏(1),…,𝐏(L)),\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{H}^{(L)}=\sum_{\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{P}^{(1)}}\cdots\sum_{\mathbf{P}^{(L)}\in\mathcal{P}^{(L)}}{{\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}{\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}}\right)}\mathbf{X}\cdot W(\mathbf{P}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{P}^{(L)})},

where the weight matrix W(𝐏(1),…,𝐏(L))=𝐖(0)𝐖(1)⋯𝐖(L)W(\mathbf{P}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{P}^{(L)})=\mathbf{W}^{(0)}\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\cdots\mathbf{W}^{(L)} for each term is a product of weight matrices at each layer and 1≤ℓ≤L\ 1\leq\ell\leq L,

𝐖(ℓ)={𝐖pos(ℓ)​𝐖cat,pos(ℓ)if 𝐏(ℓ)=Jℓα​(𝐀+^),𝐖neg(ℓ)​𝐖cat,neg(ℓ)if 𝐏(ℓ)=Jℓα​(𝐀−^),𝐖org(ℓ)​𝐖cat,org(ℓ)otherwise.\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{pos}}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{cat},\text{pos}}&\text{if $\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}=J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}^{+}})$,}\\ \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{neg}}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{cat},\text{neg}}&\text{if $\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}=J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}^{-}})$,}\\ \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{org}}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\text{cat},\text{org}}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Particularly, 𝐙\mathbf{Z} can be decomposed into a sum of 3K3^{K} different terms, each of which applies KK operators (spectral filters Jℓα​(𝐀^+)J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+}), Jℓα​(𝐀^−)J^{\alpha}_{\ell}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-}) or identity mapping 𝐈\mathbf{I}) 𝐏(1)⋯𝐏(L)\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\cdots\mathbf{P}^{(L)} over initial node features 𝐗\mathbf{X} followed by a linear transformation with unique weights W⁡(𝐏(1),…,𝐏(L))W(\mathbf{P}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{P}^{(L)}). Such a sophisticated combination empowers GegenNet to comprehensively and accurately extract and encode the sign-aware topological features in SBGs.

4.3. Spectral Feature Initialization

In lieu of learning node representations 𝐙\mathbf{Z} from randomly initialized node features 𝐗\mathbf{X}, GegenNet resorts to extracting structural semantics underlying the input topology of SBG 𝒢\mathcal{G} as the initial node feature matrix 𝐗∈ℝ(|𝒰|+|𝒱|)×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{(|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|)\times d}. Recall that the nodes in 𝒢\mathcal{G} are partitioned into 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} by their heterogeneous sources. Intuitively, 𝐗\mathbf{X} should capture not only the inter-partition relations, i.e., proximity of nodes across 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}, but also the intra-partition relations, i.e., similarities of nodes within the same partition. For ease of notation, we use 𝐔\mathbf{U} (resp. 𝐕\mathbf{V}) to represent the feature vectors of nodes in 𝒰\mathcal{U} (resp. 𝒱\mathcal{V}). Accordingly, 𝐗=[𝐔𝐕]\footnotesize\textstyle\mathbf{X}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{U}\\ \mathbf{V}\end{array}\right].

Inter-Partition Relation Preservation. First, we formulate our objective function for preserving the inter-partition relations into 𝐔\mathbf{U} and 𝐕\mathbf{V} as follows:

(12) min⁡∑(ui,vj)∈ℰ(+)𝐔∈ℝ|𝒰|×d𝐕∈ℝ|𝒱|×d⁡‖𝐔ui−𝐕vj‖22−∑(ui,vj)∈ℰ(−)‖𝐔ui−𝐕vj‖22,\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{U}|\times d}\\ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}\end{subarray}}\sum_{(u_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E}^{(+)}}{\|\mathbf{U}_{u_{i}}-\mathbf{V}_{v_{j}}\|^{2}_{2}}-\sum_{(u_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E}^{(-)}}{\|\mathbf{U}_{u_{i}}-\mathbf{V}_{v_{j}}\|^{2}_{2}},

which is to minimize the embedding distance of nodes in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} with positive links and maximize their distance with negative links. Let 𝐋\mathbf{L} be the Laplacian matrix of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, i.e., 𝐋=𝐃−𝐀~\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{D}-\tilde{\mathbf{A}}, where 𝐃\mathbf{D} stands for a (|𝒰|+|𝒱|)2(|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|)^{2} diagonal matrix whose each diagonal element 𝐃x,x=∑y∈𝒰∪𝒱𝐀~x,y\mathbf{D}_{x,x}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{V}}{\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{x,y}}. Based thereon, we can rewrite the above objective in the following equivalent form:

(13) min⁡∑ui∈|𝒰|,vj∈|𝒱|𝐗∈ℝ(|𝒰|+|𝒱|)×d⁡𝐀~ui,vj⋅‖𝐗ui−𝐗vj‖22=trace⁡(𝐗⊤​𝐋𝐗).\min_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{(|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|)\times d}}\sum_{u_{i}\in|\mathcal{U}|,v_{j}\in|\mathcal{V}|}{\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{u_{i},v_{j}}\cdot\|\mathbf{X}_{u_{i}}-\mathbf{X}_{v_{j}}\|^{2}_{2}}=\Tr(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{X}).

Intra-Partition Relation Preservation. Next, we encode the inter-partition relations of nodes into the feature vectors 𝐗\mathbf{X}. We define the intra-partition similarity of any node pair ui,uj∈𝒰u_{i},u_{j}\in\mathcal{U} by

(14) s⁡(ui,uj)=𝐀ui(+)⋅𝐀uj(+)+𝐀ui(−)⋅𝐀uj(−)|𝒩(+)|ui+|𝒩(−)|ui​|𝒩(+)|uj+|𝒩(−)|uj,\begin{gathered}\textstyle s(u_{i},u_{j})=\frac{\mathbf{A}^{(+)}_{u_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{A}^{(+)}_{u_{j}}+\mathbf{A}^{(-)}_{u_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{A}^{(-)}_{u_{j}}}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}^{(+)}|_{u_{i}}+|\mathcal{N}^{(-)}|_{u_{i}}}\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}^{(+)}|_{u_{j}}+|\mathcal{N}^{(-)}|_{u_{j}}}},\end{gathered}

where 𝐀ui(+)⋅𝐀uj(+)\mathbf{A}^{(+)}_{u_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{A}^{(+)}_{u_{j}} + 𝐀ui(−)⋅𝐀uj(−)\mathbf{A}^{(-)}_{u_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{A}^{(-)}_{u_{j}} denotes the total amount of nodes in 𝒱\mathcal{V} that directly connect to both uiu_{i} and uju_{j}, and the denominator signifies a normalization. To explain, if we regard 𝒰\mathcal{U} as users, 𝒱\mathcal{V} as movies, and ℰ(+)\mathcal{E}^{(+)}/ℰ(−)\mathcal{E}^{(-)} as likes and dislikes of users to movies, s⁡(ui,uj)s(u_{i},u_{j}) quantifies the similarity of the preferences of uiu_{i} and uju_{j} on movies. In the same vein, we can define the intra-partition similarity s⁡(vi,vj)s(v_{i},v_{j}) of any node pair vi,vj∈𝒱v_{i},v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}.

We then formulate our second objective function for capturing the inter-partition similarity of homogeneous nodes in 𝐔\mathbf{U} and 𝐕\mathbf{V} as

min⁡∑ui,uj∈𝒰𝐔∈ℝ|𝒰|×d𝐕∈ℝ|𝒱|×d⁡s⁡(ui,uj)⋅‖𝐔i−𝐔j‖22+∑vi,vj∈𝒱s⁡(vi,vj)⋅‖𝐕i−𝐕j‖22−(∑ui,uj∈𝒰s⁡(ui,uj)⋅‖𝐔i‖22+∑vi,vj∈𝒱s⁡(vi,vj)⋅‖𝐕i‖22).\begin{split}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{U}|\times d}\\ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}\end{subarray}}\sum_{u_{i},u_{j}\in\mathcal{U}}{s(u_{i},u_{j})\cdot\|\mathbf{U}_{i}-\mathbf{U}_{j}\|^{2}_{2}}+\sum_{v_{i},v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}{s(v_{i},v_{j})\cdot\|\mathbf{V}_{i}-\mathbf{V}_{j}\|^{2}_{2}}\\ -\left(\sum_{u_{i},u_{j}\in\mathcal{U}}{{s(u_{i},u_{j})}\cdot\|\mathbf{U}_{i}\|^{2}_{2}}+\sum_{v_{i},v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}{{s(v_{i},v_{j})}\cdot\|\mathbf{V}_{i}\|^{2}_{2}}\right).\end{split}

The former two terms seek to enforce homogeneous nodes with high similarities to be close in the feature space, whereas the latter ones are two regularization terms.

Let 𝐁(r){\mathbf{B}}^{(r)} and 𝐁(c){\mathbf{B}}^{(c)} be matrices obtained by applying L2L_{2} normalization to the rows and columns of the bi-adjacency matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}, respectively. It is easy to verify that s⁡(ui,uj)=𝐁ui(r)⋅𝐁uj(r)​and​s​(vi,vj)=𝐁vi(c)⋅𝐁vj(c)s(u_{i},u_{j})={\mathbf{B}}^{(r)}_{u_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{B}^{(r)}_{u_{j}}\ \text{and}\ s(v_{i},v_{j})={\mathbf{B}}^{(c)}_{v_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{B}^{(c)}_{v_{j}}. Accordingly, we define 𝐁\mathbf{B} as (0𝐁(r)𝐁(c)0)\footnotesize\begin{pmatrix}\begin{matrix}\mbox{\Large 0}\end{matrix}&\hskip-5.0pt\vline\hskip-5.0pt&{\mathbf{B}}^{(r)}\\ \hline\cr{\mathbf{B}}^{(c)}&\hskip-5.0pt\vline\hskip-5.0pt&\begin{matrix}\mbox{\Large 0}\end{matrix}\end{pmatrix}.

(15) max𝐗∈ℝ(|𝒰|+|𝒱|)×d⁡trace⁡(𝐗⊤​𝐁𝐁⊤​𝐗)\max_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{(|\mathcal{U}|+|\mathcal{V}|)\times d}}{\Tr(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{X})}

Eq. (15) states that the above objective function is equivalent to a trace maximization problem.

Spectral Decomposition. The joint optimization of Eq. (13) and Eq. (15) for the computation of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is time-consuming due to the materialization of 𝐁𝐁⊤\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top} and numerous iterations needed for convergence. As a remedy, we additionally incorporate an orthogonal constraint on 𝐗\mathbf{X} to facilitate the problem transformation and reduction. More precisely, we require the columns (i.e., feature dimensions) in 𝐗\mathbf{X} to be orthogonal to each other. In doing so, the feature dimensions of 𝐗\mathbf{X} are made decorrelate from each other, and thus, can embody richer structural information.

Theorem 4.3 (Ky Fan’s trace minimization principle (Fan, 1949)).

Given a symmetric real matrix 𝐌∈ℝn×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with distinct eigenvalues λ1​(𝐌)\lambda_{1}(\mathbf{M}), λ2​(𝐌)\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{M}), ⋯\cdots, λn​(𝐌)\lambda_{n}(\mathbf{M}), sorted by algebraic value in ascending order, eigenvectors 𝚼\boldsymbol{\Upsilon} and integer d≤nd\leq n, we have

(16) min𝐗⊤​𝐗=𝐈k⁡trace⁡(𝐗⊤​𝐌𝐗)=trace⁡(𝚼⊤​𝐌​𝚼)=∑i=1dλi​(𝐌).\textstyle\min_{\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I}_{k}}{\Tr(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X})}={\Tr(\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Upsilon})}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\lambda_{i}(\mathbf{M})}.

By Ky Fan’s trace minimization principle in Theorem 4.3, the optimal 𝐗\mathbf{X} to Eq. (13) is the eigenvectors 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} corresponding to the dd-smallest eigenvalues of 𝐋\mathbf{L}. Analogously, Eq. (15) is to find the dd-largest eigenvectors 𝚿\boldsymbol{\Psi} of 𝐁𝐁⊤\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top}, which are exactly the top-dd left singular vectors of 𝐁\mathbf{B} according to Lemma 4.4.

Lemma 4.4.

Let the columns of 𝚿{\boldsymbol{\Psi}} and 𝛂\boldsymbol{\alpha} be the dd-largest eigenvectors of 𝐁𝐁⊤\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top} and the top-dd left singular vectors of 𝐁\mathbf{B}, respectively. Then, 𝚿=𝛂\boldsymbol{\Psi}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}.

As such, the resulting feature vectors 𝐗\mathbf{X} of nodes are simply an amalgam of 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} and 𝚿\boldsymbol{\Psi}. Particularly, we combine the features from inter-partition and intra-partition relations using a weight μ\mu as in

(17) 𝐗=μ⋅𝚽+(1−μ)⋅𝚿.\mathbf{X}=\mu\cdot\boldsymbol{\Phi}+(1-\mu)\cdot\boldsymbol{\Psi}.

4.4. Model Training

After obtaining 𝐙\mathbf{Z}, we employ a 2-layer MLP to estimate the sign score yp​r​e​dy_{pred} between any two nodes ui∈𝒰u_{i}\in\mathcal{U} and vj∈𝒱v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}:

(18) yp​r​e​d=sigmoid​(MLP​(𝐙ui∥𝐙vj)).y_{pred}=\textsf{sigmoid}(\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{Z}_{u_{i}}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{Z}_{v_{j}})).

Particularly, the larger the yp​r​e​dy_{pred} is, the higher the probability that the edge sign is positive. Contrarily, the smaller yp​r​e​dy_{pred} is, the higher the probability that the edge sign is negative. Following previous work (Huang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2023), we adopt the cross-entropy as the loss function for the link sign prediction task, which is formulated as

(19) ℒ=−y⋅log(yp​r​e​d)+(1−y)⋅log(1−yp​r​e​d),\mathcal{L}=-y\cdot\log{(y_{pred})}+(1-y)\cdot\log{\left(1-y_{pred}\right)},

where yy is the ground truth mapped from {−1,1}\{-1,1\} to {0,1}\{0,1\}.

5. Experiments

This section empirically evaluates the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in link sign classification on six real SBG datasets (Huang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2023) from various application domains. The statistics of the datasets are summarized in Table 3. We randomly split all edges into training, cross-validation, and test sets with an 8:1:18:1:1 ratio. For a robust and fair evaluation, all experiments are conducted on a Linux machine equipped with 4 AMD EPYC 7313 CPUs (500GB RAM) and 1 NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU (24GB memory). The codebase and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/wanghewen/GegenNet.

5.1. Baselines and Hyperparameters

We compare GegenNet against 11 competitors, including MSGNN (He et al., 2022a), SDGNN (Huang et al., 2021c), SGCN (Derr et al., 2018), SiGAT (Huang et al., 2019b), SigMaNet (Fiorini et al., 2023), SNEA (Li et al., 2020b), SSSNET (He et al., 2022c), SBGCL (Zhang et al., 2023), SBGNN (Huang et al., 2021a), SidNet (Jung et al., 2022), SLGNN (Li et al., 2023), in terms of edge classification accuracy. For MSGNN, SDGNN, SGCN, SiGAT, SigMaNet, SNEA and SSSNET, we leverage the implementation in (He et al., 2022a). For SBGCL, SBGNN, SidNet, and SLGNN, we use the source codes from the respective authors. The embedding size of the node is set to 32, and the maximum training epochs to 300 in different methods. For the rest of the parameters, we adopt the parameter settings suggested in their respective papers. For GegenNet, we set the learning rate to be 0.01, dropout rate to be 0.5, weight decay to be 1e-5, weight parameter μ\mu to be 0.3, the number of model layers LL to be 3, and SVD dimension dd to be 32.

5.2. Link Sign Prediction Performance

We evaluate the performance of GegenNet on the link sign prediction task, with results presented in Table 4 in terms of AUC and F1-score. GegenNet consistently outperforms existing methods across all datasets, effectively capturing both the structural properties and sign dynamics inherent to signed bipartite graphs. For datasets where certain methods encounter errors during execution or fail to converge, the results are excluded and marked as “-” in Table 4.

GegenNet achieves significant improvements over baseline models. On all six datasets, GegenNet yields the highest AUC and F1 scores. Such results highlight the model’s robustness in learning nuanced positive and negative relationships while preserving the bipartite structure. A key factor contributing to GegenNet ’s success is its novel spectral filtering mechanism based on Gegenbauer polynomials, which offers better expressiveness for both low- and high-frequency graph signals. Compared to alternative spectral bases like Chebyshev or Legendre polynomials, the Gegenbauer-based filtering with α=1.5\alpha=1.5 consistently demonstrates superior adaptability to the graph signal distributions.

Furthermore, GegenNet shows strong resilience on sparse and imbalanced datasets. For example, the Bonanza dataset contains very few negative links, while the Review dataset is characterized by sparsely connected nodes. Despite these challenges, GegenNet maintains robust performance, achieving competitive AUC and F1 scores where other methods tend to struggle. Overall, GegenNet’s design effectively preserves the bipartite graph structure and distinguishes between positive and negative relationships during spectral convolutions. By modeling both inter- and intra-partition proximities, GegenNet captures comprehensive graph information, leading to significant improvements in link sign prediction.

5.3. Ablation Study

Table 5 presents the ablation study results, evaluating the impact of spectral transformations (ST), as well as random embeddings, on the performance of the GegenNet model. The full GegenNet model, incorporating both positive and negative spectral transformations, consistently achieves superior performance. For instance, in the Amazon dataset, the Chebyshev-based model attains an AUC of 0.8006 and an F1 score of 0.6834. Omitting the negative ST results in a significant decline to an AUC of 0.7687 and an F1 score of 0.6643. Similarly, in the Bonanza dataset, the AUC of model with α=1.5\alpha=1.5 decreases from 0.7301 to 0.6500 upon removal of the negative ST. Notably, the negative spectral transformation has a more pronounced effect on performance. In the Bonanza dataset, with α=1.5\alpha=1.5, eliminating the negative ST leads to a sharp AUC reduction from 0.7301 to 0.6500, underscoring its critical role in capturing structural and signed relationships within the graph. In contrast, removing the positive ST results in a smaller performance decline. Introducing random embeddings, devoid of spectral transformations, leads to the most severe performance degradation across all datasets. In the MLM dataset, substituting learned embeddings with random ones reduces the AUC from 0.8074 to 0.7324. In summary, both positive and negative spectral transformations are vital for optimal performance. Replacing spectral transformations with random embeddings substantially degrades performance, emphasizing the importance of spectral learning in capturing meaningful graph structures and enhancing link sign prediction accuracy.

5.4. Hyperparameter Analysis

Figure 2 demonstrates that the choice of μ\mu and the type of basis function significantly impact the model’s performance (as measured by AUC). There is a consistent trend of performance degradation as μ\mu increases beyond 0.7 for all datasets and basis functions. The results suggest that optimal μ\mu values are dataset-dependent, but generally lie between 0.1 and 0.5 across different datasets.

Figure 3 shows that different datasets exhibit varying levels of sensitivity to changes in the number of transformation layers in GegenNet. For Amazon, Bonanza, and Review, the AUC shows significant fluctuations, while House1to10, MLM, and Senate exhibit more stable behavior. When α=1.5\alpha=1.5, model tends to outperform the other two basis functions in datasets such as Bonanza and MLM, but Chebyshev is able to achieve the best results in datasets like House1to10 and Review. The optimal number of transformation layers varies by dataset and basis function, underscoring the importance of dataset-specific tuning.

Figure 4 illustrates how model performance changes as the SVD dimension increases. Note that the number of nodes must be less than the SVD dimension, so in the Review and Senate datasets, the SVD dimension is truncated to 128. Across all datasets, increasing the SVD dimension generally leads to improved AUC, with the highest performance typically observed between 242^{4} and 272^{7}. In Amazon, Bonanza, and Review, performance consistently improves with higher SVD dimensions, while in House1to10, MLM, and Senate, performance stabilizes after a certain point, with only minor gains beyond that. These results emphasize the importance of selecting an appropriate SVD dimension for each dataset, as overfitting may occur at higher dimensions in some cases.

6. Conclusion

This paper presents GegenNet, a spectral convolutional neural network tailored for signed bipartite graphs. By leveraging Gegenbauer polynomials for spectral filtering, GegenNet effectively captures both low- and high-frequency graph signals. Experiments across six real-world datasets demonstrate its superiority in link sign prediction tasks compared to existing models. Ablation studies further confirm the critical role of both positive and negative spectral transformations in enhancing performance. Future work may explore extending GegenNet to dynamic or multiplex bipartite networks to handle temporal information and multiple interaction types.

(20) Jkα​(λ)=∑i=0⌊k2⌋(−1)i​(α)k−i(1)i​(1)k−2​i⋅(2​λ)k−2​i.\textstyle J^{\alpha}_{k}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}{(-1)^{i}\frac{(\alpha)_{k-i}}{(1)_{i}(1)_{k-2i}}\cdot(2\lambda)^{k-2i}}.

Jkα​(𝐀^+)\displaystyle\textstyle J^{\alpha}_{k}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+}) =𝐔+⋅Jkα​(𝚲+)⋅𝐔+⊤=𝐔+​∑i=0⌊k2⌋(−1)i​(α)k−i(1)i​(1)k−2​i​(2​𝚲+)k−2​i​𝐔+⊤\displaystyle\textstyle=\mathbf{U}^{+}\cdot J^{\alpha}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{+})\cdot{\mathbf{U}^{+}}^{\top}=\mathbf{U}^{+}\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}{(-1)^{i}\frac{(\alpha)_{k-i}}{(1)_{i}(1)_{k-2i}}(2\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{+})^{k-2i}}{\mathbf{U}^{+}}^{\top}
=∑i=0⌊k2⌋(−1)i(α)k−i(1)i​(1)k−2​i2k−2​i⋅𝐀^+k−2​i.\displaystyle\textstyle=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}(-1)^{i}\frac{(\alpha)_{k-i}}{(1)_{i}(1)_{k-2i}}2^{k-2i}\cdot{\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{+^{k-2i}}}.

In the same vein, Jkα(𝐀^−)=∑i=0⌊k2⌋(−1)i(α)k−i(1)i​(1)k−2​i2k−2​i⋅𝐀^−k−2​iJ^{\alpha}_{k}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-})=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}(-1)^{i}\frac{(\alpha)_{k-i}}{(1)_{i}(1)_{k-2i}}2^{k-2i}\cdot{\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{-^{k-2i}}}.
